I've learned to slow down, appreciate my friends and family more, and open my eyes wider and observe things more closely. Just the other day I spent an hour observing a crow. Anxiety is difficult to manage, but one method that worked very well for me and others, is to acknowledge your worries but instead of getting stuck thinking about it, you decide that you will worry a lot, but later during the day. Lets say at 7pm for 45 minutes, it's important to have the time. At 7pm you will worry a lot about everything. Then you can move on. Worrying a few hours later won't change anything. If you have more worries during the day, those too could be considered in great length at 7pm. When 7pm comes, you can then feel extra anxious, you have dedicated time for that. Sometimes it's 7pm and you have a lot of worries to consider, but you don't want to think about them. You moved on. "There will always be causes for anxiety, whether due to prosperity or to wretchedness," like Seneca said. Instead accept that sometimes you will feel anxious, but try to focus on sparking other, more positive feelings that you're looking for. If the anxiety is a problem, look for help learning to cope with it (I like Dr. K's Healthy Gamer videos), but if you're an anxious person like me, don't trick yourself into thinking it'll suddenly disappear some day. 2. In regard to sparking those positive feelings, don't try to make it happen intellectually. Do things. Try stuff out. Treat it as an exploration. Your brain will have one reaction to thinking about something and another to actually doing it. You want to test things and then pay attention and see if they actually spark positive feelings for you. One thing I was sure I would enjoy was volunteer work. I did a bunch of nonprofit volunteering during my free weekends for a few months. Turns out I wasn't a great fit for the ones I tried and didn't super enjoy it. I still admire those organizations and care about what they do, but I feel better giving them monetary support and using my free time doing other things. If I had never actually gone and volunteered, I would have sat around thinking "oh if only I dedicate myself to some great purpose will I be happy." Doing things helped me actually learn about myself. 3. This is sort of an extension of #1, but don't aim for some blissful, uncomplicated future. Almost certainly your whole life—past, present, and future—was, is, and will be some mix of good and bad. We're awash in an achievement, media, and advertising culture that promises us one day all of our problems will be solved. None of that is to say you can't take action in your life and change things, and the end result of those changes may improve the balance, but we all still get old, we all die, tragedies will happen. That's just part of the human condition. But so is fun, joy, curiosity, friendship. So make the most of the good, accept the bad, change what you can, and let go of the idea of total control. That's what's worked for me anyway. reply ChrisMarshallNY 3 hours ago | prev | next [–] 41? You're still a kid. I'm 64.
